overview: Anguilla’s history includes Indigenous settlements, plantation slavery, seafaring communities and resistance to government from Saint Kitts. Archaeological remains and local records connect these political changes with water, work and cultural life.

periods.title: Water and ceremony at Fountain Cavern
periods.summary: Pottery and radiocarbon evidence indicate use of Fountain Cavern around or before 400 CE through at least 1200. Carvings and serving vessels suggest ceremonial activity alongside access to freshwater.

periods.title: Plantations and enslaved labor
periods.summary: Hughes Estate preserves structures associated with sugar production, water collection and domestic work. Research combines these remains with records of the people enslaved on the property.

periods.title: Farming, migration and mutual support
periods.summary: After emancipation, households cultivated small plots and some people sought work elsewhere in the Caribbean. Remittances, locally built boats and shared labor connected family survival with regional movement.

periods.title: Federation and contested association
periods.summary: Saint Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla joined the West Indies Federation in 1958. Its collapse in 1962 left unresolved questions about government and the relationship among the islands.

periods.title: The Anguilla Revolution
periods.summary: Anguillians expelled the Saint Kitts police in May 1967. British intervention and further negotiations followed as the island sought separation from the associated state.

periods.title: A separate British territory
periods.summary: Anguilla became a separate dependent territory in December 1980. This changed its administration without establishing a sovereign independent country.

periods.title: Documenting buildings and recovering histories
periods.summary: A historical register, archival cataloging and excavation at Hughes Estate have broadened the evidence available for Anguilla’s past. Community organizations participate in preserving and interpreting this heritage.

items.text: At Fountain Cavern, people carved faces and other forms into natural stalagmites. One figure has been interpreted as Jocahu, known from accounts of Indigenous Caribbean religion. That identification is an interpretation, while the worked stone itself is direct evidence of skilled engagement with the cave’s natural surfaces.

Fragments of large open bowls were recovered above the cave’s first pool. Their forms and setting support an interpretation involving ceremonial serving as well as water collection. Later Anguillians also collected freshwater here, and a ladder installed in 1953 made descent easier than the older route using tree roots.

The 2021 Hughes Estate team recorded ship drawings inside a building tentatively identified as a smokehouse. Enslaved people worked there, but the carvings’ precise meanings remain uncertain. They may relate to maritime connections or aspirations for freedom; they cannot by themselves identify a particular escape or its participants.

At the estate’s cistern, Aveline Wilson measured a plastered platform sloping toward the water store. This supports its interpretation as a rainwater catchment. The finding reveals a practical response to water supply while leaving other questions open, including the identities of people who occupied nearby rooms.

The cultural-policy history describes neighbors sharing a burning stick when a household needed to light its cooking fire. Such exchanges mattered where matches and cash could be scarce. This remembered practice makes mutual support visible in an ordinary task, without implying that every family had the same resources or experience.

Jollification brought people together for work with food, music and sociability. The policy’s examples include preparing planting grounds, launching wooden vessels and moving houses. Participants supplied labor without wages, while shared meals supported the gathering. It was a way of organizing demanding tasks through community relationships.

The historical society preserves captions for Anne Bailey’s photographs of people collecting salt at Sandy Ground in 1976, alongside views of the Road Bay saltpans. These dated records place salt work within living memory. They do not, on their own, establish workers’ pay, production totals or when the industry began.

sections.title: Boatbuilding, travel and records of the sea

items.text: The society’s maritime gallery identifies Warspite as a wooden vessel built in 1902 and also records schooner construction, interisland ferries and race preparations. These examples show different uses of maritime skill. A trading ship, a passenger ferry and a racing boat should not be treated as interchangeable craft.

Sombrero Lighthouse records include keepers’ journals and a provision ledger covering 1897 to 1916. Preserved through the Endangered Archives Programme, they offer evidence for the routine organization behind navigation. The catalog establishes that these records survive; particular meals, weather observations or incidents require consulting their individual pages.

The National Trust presents David Carty’s Nuttin Bafflin as a documentary connecting boat racing with Anguillian history and identity. Its preservation work places racing alongside historical buildings and oral traditions. This recognizes sporting knowledge as part of cultural heritage, not simply as entertainment for visitors.

Anguilla Day commemorates 30 May 1967, when Anguillians forced the Saint Kitts police to leave. Negotiations over the island’s separation continued afterward. The anniversary marks a decisive political action, not the date on which Anguilla became an internationally recognized independent state.

The historical register established in 2007 records sites ranging from Indigenous settlement remains to plantation estates and wooden houses. Cataloging these different places helps make everyday buildings part of the historical record. It also provides information for protection without assuming that inclusion guarantees a building’s survival.

ending.text: Anguilla became a separate British dependent territory on 19 December 1980. It continues as a territory administered by the United Kingdom and remains on the UN decolonization list. The map’s endpoint in 2020 marks its coverage, not Anguilla’s disappearance or a declaration of independence.
